meta.title: Who really said "The longer I live, the more I am inclined to the belief that this earth is used by other planets as a lunatic asylum"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Attributed to Shaw, but on one man's word: Judge Henry Neil's September 1919 letter. The line is in no known Shaw work, and Voltaire got there first.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The longer I live, the more I am inclined to the belief that this earth is used by other planets as a lunatic asylum'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed, not verified. It surfaces in a September 1919 newspaper letter reporting Shaw's private correspondence about widows' pensions.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Shaw, and entirely in character — but the whole case rests on one report. In September 1919 Judge Henry Neil, an American campaigner for pensions for widowed mothers, told newspapers that Shaw had written this to him in private correspondence. No play, preface, published letter or other work of Shaw’s has been found containing the sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes Shaw probably did use it, while noting the claim depends on Neil’s veracity.

source.excerpt: The longer I live, the more I am inclined to the belief that this earth is used by other planets as a lunatic asylum.
trail: 1747–1749 — the conceit is already old. Edward Young calls Earth “the Bedlam of the universe”, and Voltaire’s Memnon fears our globe is the mad-house of a hundred thousand million worlds: QI’s Voltaire article ↗.

September 1919 — Judge Henry Neil’s letter reports the Shaw wording, running in Dublin, London and New York within a fortnight: QI’s Shaw chronology ↗. Notably, the London weekly The Nation had itself printed the same conceit in 1917, before it printed the Shaw version.

1920–1921 — the line detaches from the pensions row and becomes a stock Shaw epigram. Patrick Gallagher’s book cites “what Mr. George Bernard Shaw calls ‘the insane asylum for all other planets’” on page 114 of the 1920 scan ↗.
1929 onward — reassignment. Mark Twain in 1929, Thomas Jefferson in the Commons in 1937, Bertrand Russell via Vonnegut in 2004: QI’s overview ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Neil gave the papers, and the one Quote Investigator calls the most common initial phrasing. The London periodical The Nation printed the same remark on 6 September 1919 with one word changed — “this sphere” for “this earth”. No fuller text of the underlying Shaw letter has been produced.
source.rightsNote: The sentence’s first documented publication is the September 1919 run of Judge Neil’s letter in the Dublin Weekly Freeman, the London Daily Herald and the New-York Tribune; text published that long ago is in the public domain in the United States. That covers only this one reported sentence as printed in 1919 — Shaw’s own later plays, prefaces and correspondence are a separate matter and remain controlled by his estate and publishers.

author.heading: George Bernard Shaw
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic & polemicist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1925
author.bio: Born in Dublin in 1856 and dead in 1950, Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic, polemicist and political activist who took the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925. He wrote Man and Superman, Pygmalion and Saint Joan, and just as prolifically wrote letters, prefaces and press interventions on socialism, vivisection, spelling reform and welfare policy. That combination — enormous fame plus an enormous, scattered, half-unpublished output — is exactly what makes him one of the internet’s favourite hosts for orphan epigrams.

misattribution.heading: The asylum quote has had at least five owners
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most heavily reassigned lines in circulation. Two problems run in parallel: Shaw did not invent the idea, and other famous names have been handed the sentence outright. Quote Investigator traces the family across more than 250 years ↗.

items.why: The English poet’s The Complaint, Or, Night-thoughts had “Or Earth; the Bedlam of the universe!” in ‘Night Nine’, serialised in The Scots Magazine in 1747 — per QI ↗.

In Memnon ou La Sagesse Humaine, published by 1749, Memnon fears “that our little terraqueous globe here is the mad-house of those hundred thousand millions of worlds” (1807 English translation) — QI’s Voltaire article ↗. Shaw’s version is a late entry in an old genre, not an invention.
A 1929 St. Louis Post-Dispatch column by Elsie McCormick called it “Mark Twain’s theory” — Twain having died in 1910. QI calls the linkage implausible and not substantive ↗.
In 1937 the MP John Leslie told the House of Commons that Jefferson had observed “this world was the lunatic asylum for other planets”. QI finds no substance in it ↗.
In a 2004 piece for In These Times, Kurt Vonnegut credited Russell with calling this planet “the lunatic asylum of the Universe” — recorded in QI’s chronology ↗, with no earlier Russell source shown.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest summary: the metaphor belongs to Young and Voltaire; the specific sentence belongs to Shaw only on the word of Judge Henry Neil in September 1919, which is why Quote Investigator says he “probably did employ this saying” rather than that he did ↗.

context.heading: Why a pensions campaigner was quoting Shaw at all
lead: The line did not arrive as an aphorism. It arrived inside an argument about money for widows. Judge Henry Neil was an American promoter of “mothers’ pensions” — cash payments to impoverished widowed mothers — and he had been corresponding with Shaw, who supported them. According to Quote Investigator’s account ↗, what struck Shaw as absurd was the willingness of lawmakers to pension war widows while refusing peace widows. It was that species of illogic, Neil said, that provoked the remark.

Neil then did what campaigners do with a good line from a famous ally: he put it in a letter to the press. In September 1919 versions of that letter ran in the Dublin Weekly Freeman, the London Daily Herald and the New-York Tribune. Within a year the sentence was loose in the wild — a 1920 book on American policy in Asia already cites “what Mr. George Bernard Shaw calls” the insane asylum for all other planets, with no mention of widows, pensions or Judge Neil at all. That is the moment a quote stops being evidence and starts being furniture.
context.detailsSummary: How solid is Judge Neil’s report?
detailsBody: It is second-hand but not anonymous. Neil named Shaw, wrote under his own name, and did so while Shaw was alive, famous and notoriously willing to correct the record in print. No repudiation from Shaw has been located. That is the strongest part of the case.

The weak part: the underlying letter itself has not been produced. Quote Investigator notes that the London periodical The Nation said Neil’s letter had appeared in the Daily News on Monday, 1 September 1919, and states it has not yet accessed that prime citation. The Nation’s own printing also differs by a word: it has “this sphere” where the other papers have “this earth” — see the QI chronology ↗.

Modern quote sites also circulate a smoothed rewrite — ‘the more convinced am I that this planet is used by other planets as a lunatic asylum’ — which matches none of the 1919 printings. If you are quoting this, quote the 1919 wording and say who reported it.
context.pull: The whole attribution rests on one campaigner’s word about a letter nobody else has produced.
